Three reviewers change it; privacy-minimality drops it along with the bank signature. Keep only the first option: record the bank by name at registration, in its own field under the digest. Never derive it from the delegation, which the stolen key alone can change (must-fix 2), and never let the request choose it. Change it only by the ⅔ name action. A later co-signature needs the bank's key unburned and the bank not frozen, but no seat; otherwise a stake dip in dynamic mode strands the bank's customers. There is no fallback to another bank. When a burned bank's name is voted to a new key, its customers follow automatically, because the field is a name. Cost: each name's bank is public through GET /hdls/accounts, much as the delegate is today.

Every reviewer who keeps a bank signature keeps A6. Privacy-minimality drops it only because it drops that signature. The co-signature needs its own domain (signing/domain.go asks for one per payload type). It must not be a conflict slot. Otherwise any customer, or a thief with a customer's key, could get an automated desk signer to co-sign two different requests and burn the bank's key. With one key per name, that key is also the bank's consensus key and its seat. Endorsing two requests is not equivocation. Because all signatures cover one preimage, a co-signature can't be reused on another request.

Attacker changes it; the other three keep it, banks-lifecycle noting that the bank is the natural requestor. With names as identity, an unnamed key can neither sign nor pay, so 'the requestor is a funded named account' already holds. Go one step further and make a registration's requestor the bank itself. It pays the fee, signs once and becomes the bank of record, and the new key's proof of possession is the second signature. That removes the requestor field and one 3.3 KB signature. It also stops a sponsor's bank from vouching for a stranger it never met and then gating that stranger's key changes. A sponsor pays the bank with an ordinary payment. This narrows your 'anyone if it was free' (see the open questions).

All four keep it, and three extend it. A burned key can be neither the holder, the co-signing bank nor the new key; otherwise any bank could give a burned key a fresh name and make it a working credential again. A new key must not be any name's current key, so a burn maps to exactly one name and no shared key links two pseudonyms. A frozen name can be neither the name nor the bank in a request. A name whose key is burned, or which is frozen, changes key only by the ⅔ name action, and such a name never counts as free (must-fix 3).

All four drop it. Nothing needs migrating: there are no users, and the ML-DSA genesis replaces every key anyway. The new genesis lists every account by name, and its validation rejects unnamed, non-canonical or duplicate names and duplicate keys. With names as identity there are no unnamed accounts, so your 'a key with no name refuses payments' needs no rule of its own. AccountUpdate's name claim becomes dead code and goes.

open_questions: Who may register a free name? I recommend only a bank: it pays, signs once and becomes the bank of record, and a sponsor pays the bank by ordinary payment. Your text says anyone, which adds a requestor field, a third signature, and a bank vouching for someone it never met.

Should a key change wait N blocks ('n frames') so it can be stopped? I recommend no protocol delay. A delay needs pending state, a maturity step and cancel rules, and it keeps a leaked key valid for N more blocks. A bank of record can impose a cooling-off for sales as policy.

Should new_key be a burn slot under your rule (two different requests signed by one key)? I recommend no. Wallets have no sign log, so retries and restored backups would burn honest keys and freeze names, and payments, the thief's real tool, still have no slot (E44).
How does a customer change banks? Only by the ⅔ name action (the smallest option), or also by a request that both the old and the new bank co-sign (one more signature and one more rule)?

Charge the fee on every key change, as you wrote, or only on registration? With a fee on every change, a theft victim whose balance was drained needs a top-up from the bank before re-keying, or the ⅔ path.

Every account now needs a bank to exist, and its bank of record is public. Will banks register pseudonymous names, for example sold for cash? docs/managing-the-currency.md:274-287 promises a prepaid-key cash path and calls 'every account forced to carry a registered identity' a surveillance smell. Those passages need rewriting either way.

Hash-of-key names: a wallet convention only, or a reserved self-certifying form? For example, 'k-' plus 26 base32 characters of the key's SHA-256, valid at registration only for the key it hashes. That is about 3 lines, and it stops anyone registering your hash name first from gossip.

Signature record: keep committed new_key requests, including the bank co-signature that shows who vouched for a key? The choices are for RetainBlocks heights, for the chain's life like governance certificates, or never, like account updates.

Phase 3: with one key per name, a bank co-signs with its consensus key, so the desk software must reach the bank's signer. Accept a signer that exposes only the new-key-bank domain to the desk, or plan a separate co-signing key per bank?

rejected.title: Free names, hash names included, can be sniped from gossip (attacker)
rejected.reason: Not kept as a must-fix. First-come is inherent to readable names. A snipe needs a dishonest bank, or one that co-signs automatically, and costs a fee and that bank's signature. It is traceable to the recorded bank and correctable by the ⅔ name vote. Intake already refuses payments to unregistered names (node/node.go:554), so nobody can pay a name before it lands, and the wallet should show a name only after /hdls/resolve confirms it. The self-certifying hash-name form is an open question.

rejected.title: The bank co-signature can be bypassed or can hold clients hostage, so drop it, the bank field, A5 and A6 (privacy-minimality)
rejected.reason: You asked for the bank's signature. The bypass that report describes, a thief picking or re-delegating to a lax bank, is closed by a bank of record. A bank that refuses or disappears blocks only key changes, not payments, and the ⅔ name action covers that case. The privacy cost is real and is listed as an open question.

rejected.title: Charging the fee lets a thief silence the victim's contest by draining first (privacy-minimality)
rejected.reason: Moot once A4's contest path is dropped. The trade-off that remains, a drained victim needing a top-up or the ⅔ path, is an open question.

rejected.title: Make BlockID an expiry sized for the bank's counter step (banks-lifecycle)
rejected.reason: An exact BlockID matches payments and updates and keeps the pool bound and the replay guard simple. An expiry lets a request replay if a name returns to an earlier key inside the window. Once A4 is dropped, a request that misses its block is signed again at no risk, and collecting all the signatures at the end of the visit fits easily in a 64-block window.

rejected.title: Keep A4's delay and judge the conflict against committed pending state (attacker, privacy-minimality)
rejected.reason: It works, but it is heavy: pending state under the digest, a maturity step, cancel and re-check rules, and a contest path. That is the notify-and-cancel feature the owner leaned against. It still leaves payments without a conflict slot and keeps a leaked key valid for N more blocks. Replaced by no delay plus the ⅔ freeze and name vote.

rejected.title: Count the fee in the overdraw sum, since a proposer could time a request to trip the ban (attacker)
rejected.reason: Not needed under the recommended rule. A request's fee payer sends no payment in that block, so the fee never enters the overdraw sum and there is nothing to time.

rejected.title: Keep every committed new_key for the life of the chain (state-transition), or never keep it (privacy-minimality)
rejected.reason: This is a retention policy, not a defect. The bank of record in state already shows who vouches for each name today. Listed as an open question.

rejected.title: Registration sets the delegate to the bank by default (state-transition)
rejected.reason: The design doesn't need it, and E42 warns against auto-delegation. Delegation stays the holder's own AccountUpdate, set through the wallet's delegate field.

rejected.title: A validator's self-re-key leaves its old-key vote in pooled certificates and spoils them (banks-lifecycle)
rejected.reason: Moot with the seat rule. A seated name changes key only by a ⅔ action, which bumps the governance sequence and retires every in-flight certificate anyway (pruneReassignments and pruneParameterProposals).
